p: Good evening. My name is Edmund Thornleigh, Doctor of Civil Law, sometime Fellow of Oriel College in the University of Oxford, and now, in this year of grace eighteen hundred and seventy-five, a retired scholar living in a tall and draughty house upon Lansdown Crescent in the city of Bath. I have a library of some eleven thousand volumes, a housekeeper named Mrs Pruett who disapproves of most of them, and an elderly spaniel named Tacitus, who sleeps by the fire and has outlived two of my critics. It is my intention, if you will permit me, to tell you the history of mankind, from its first uncertain steps upon the plains of Africa to an age of thinking engines which no person now living in Bath has any reason to expect.

I should explain at once how a man writing in eighteen seventy-five can speak of events that have not yet occurred. I cannot explain it fully, and I have given up trying. Some years ago there began to arrive upon my desk, generally in the small hours and always without a postmark, the pages of a great Encyclopaedia of the future, composed, so far as I can tell, by a multitude of anonymous hands in the early part of the twenty-first century. Its authors are diligent, quarrelsome and, on the whole, admirably honest about the limits of their knowledge. I have read it as a historian reads any source: gratefully, and with suspicion. Where I speak of the great wars of the twentieth century, of the splitting of the atom, or of the calculating machines which now converse, I am relying upon that Encyclopaedia and upon other honest works that have reached me by the same mysterious post. I shall not pretend to have seen these things. I shall tell you what the record says, and what, as an old man who has spent his life among the ruins of empires, I think of it.

You will hear two kinds of piece. The first are my own essays, written in my own words, in which I attempt to tell the story of some great turning point in the affairs of mankind: the taming of fire, the invention of writing, the fall of Rome, the coming of the steam engine, and so on. The second are readings from the Encyclopaedia of the future itself. These are not my words. They were written by its many authors and are given to you, faithfully, under the terms of their licence, which requires that they be credited and shared alike. I introduce each reading, I occasionally interrupt it with a remark of my own, and I always tell you when it ends. I have adapted them only for the ear: I have omitted passages that merely list foreign names or the spelling of words in alphabets you cannot see, and I have written our dates in the old fashion, B C and A D, which is how I was taught and how I shall die.

You may hear these pieces in several orders. There is a Grand Chronological Journey, which begins in the remotest past and ends with the thinking machines. There are journeys by theme: inventions, habits and customs, beliefs and ideas, empires and wars, science and medicine, trade and money, the deep origins of mankind, people, and places. And there is a long shuffle, for the evenings when you would rather be surprised. None of them requires you to touch anything once it has begun. I shall simply go on talking, which, Mrs Pruett will tell you, is my natural condition.

A historian is a man who has agreed to be disappointed. The past does not arrange itself for our convenience; the documents are lost, the witnesses lied, and the most important things, the habits of ordinary people, were too obvious for anyone to write down. I shall therefore tell you, as often as honesty requires, where the evidence is firm and where it is thin. For the deepest ages, before writing, we have only bones, stones, seeds and the ashes of ancient fires, and the learned men who interpret them disagree with a vigour that does them credit. I shall give you their best opinions, and I shall not dress up a conjecture as a certainty.

I shall also try never to leave you stranded in a foreign tongue. It is the vice of my profession to scatter Latin and French through an English sentence like currants through a cake, and to assume that every reader has eaten the same cake. Whenever I quote a phrase in another language, I shall tell you at once what it means. If I mention a book, I shall tell you who wrote it and what manner of book it is. And I shall keep numbers to the few that matter, for history is not a ledger, though it is sometimes kept like one.

Every historian has prejudices, and the honest ones confess them. I admire Mr Edward Gibbon, author of The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, the greatest work of history in our language, whose irony I have tried to imitate and whose certainty I have tried to avoid. I distrust conquerors, though I find them interesting. I believe that the plough, the alphabet and the drain have done more for mankind than all the battles ever fought, though I shall describe a good many battles, because they were fought, and because the people who died in them deserve to be remembered. I was raised in the Church of England and have spent my life studying the faiths of other peoples; I shall speak of all religions with the respect due to the deepest hopes of mankind and with the candour due to a historical record.

The pages from the future have obliged me to revise some of my opinions. I had supposed, as most men of my age suppose, that the progress of the nineteenth century would carry on smoothly, like a well-made railway, toward universal comfort and peace. The Encyclopaedia informs me that the railway passes through some very dark country indeed. I shall not spare you that country. Nor shall I spare you the astonishing achievements on the far side of it.
Settle yourself, then. Tacitus has already done so. We begin, as all things begin, in darkness, a very long time ago.
